t: Maximum Number of Non-Overlapping Substrings — Editorial
o: We must partition parts of `s` into as many disjoint substrings as possible, where each chosen substring is 'closed': every character appearing in it has **all** its occurrences inside it. Ties in count are broken by minimum total length. In example 1 (`adefaddaccc`), the letter `a` forces any substring containing `a` to span indices 0–7, so taking anything containing `a` wastes space; instead we pick the tiny closed pieces `e`, `f`, and `ccc`. In example 2 (`abbaccd`), both `["d","abba","cc"]` and `["d","bb","cc"]` give 3 substrings, but the latter has smaller total length, so we prefer short closed pieces over long ones whenever both are available. With n up to 1e5, an O(n·26) or O(n log n) solution is expected; a brute force over all substrings is far too slow.
k: For each character, only its first and last occurrence matter: a valid substring starting at i containing c must extend at least to last[c].
A substring s[i..j] is valid iff every character inside it has first[c] >= i and last[c] <= j.
After collecting candidate intervals, a classic greedy 'sort by right endpoint, take non-overlapping' maximizes the count; preferring shorter intervals preserves optimality of total length.

a.i: For every index i, try to build the smallest valid substring starting at i: repeatedly extend the right end to cover the last occurrence of any new character seen, until stable. If during expansion the window reaches before i (some character occurs earlier), the start i is invalid. Each expansion pass costs O(n) per attempt but stabilizes quickly since each extension jumps to a fixed last[] position; overall this is O(26n) after memoizing per-character results. The resulting candidate intervals are then resolved greedily.
s: Precompute first[c] and last[c] for each letter.
For each start i, expand j = max(last[c]) over characters in s[i..j]; if some first[c] < i, mark i invalid.
Sort intervals by right endpoint (then by length ascending).
Greedily pick intervals whose start > previous picked end; append corresponding substrings.
a.t: O(n · 26) worst case — each start expands through at most 26 distinct characters using precomputed first/last arrays.
a.sp: O(n) for the result plus O(26) auxiliary arrays.

a.n: Approach 2: Candidate Intervals + Greedy by Right Endpoint (Optimal)
a.i: Instead of expanding from scratch, note a valid interval starting at i must have j >= last[s[i]], and it is valid iff scanning i..j keeps every character's first[c] >= i and last[c] <= j. We compute one minimal candidate per feasible start in O(n), then apply the classic activity-selection greedy: sort candidates by right endpoint and take each interval that starts after the previously taken end. Because ties in count are broken by total length, and shorter intervals ending no later never reduce future choices, this greedy also yields minimum total length.
s: Precompute first[c] and last[c] for all 26 letters.
For each index i, set j = last[s[i]]; while scanning k from i to j, update j = max(j, last[s[k]]); if any first[s[k]] < i, discard this start.
Collect each surviving interval [i, j] as a candidate.
Sort candidates by right endpoint (break ties by left endpoint descending so shorter wins).
Greedily take candidates with start > lastEnd, appending their substrings.
a.t: O(n log n) — building candidates is O(n·26); sorting up to n candidates dominates.
a.sp: O(n) for the candidate list and output.

w: In an interview, go straight to Approach 2: precompute first/last occurrences, derive minimal valid intervals, then run the classic 'earliest finishing interval' greedy — it signals familiarity with activity selection. Common pitfalls: forgetting that a valid window may need to grow *after* seeing a later character (the inner while must re-check last[] as j grows), overlapping checks off-by-one (use strict `start > prevEnd`), and ignoring the minimum-total-length tie-break (sort by end, then prefer shorter). Edge cases: single-character strings (answer is that character), strings where one letter spans everything (answer is the whole string), and repeated letters like "aaaa". Follow-ups might ask to return the maximum count only (drop the tie-break), or to handle larger alphabets (replace fixed 26-arrays with hash maps).
